claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 normally requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Approximately 5 wt% elemental silicon is added to the ZrB2 powder before sintering.
The Si-containing ZrB2 can be processed near 2000 °C under an inert or vacuum atmosphere.
Silicon reacts at high temperature to form a transient liquid phase during ZrB2 sintering.
The transient liquid phase enhances particle rearrangement.
The transient liquid phase improves grain-boundary wetting.
Transient-liquid-assisted rearrangement, wetting, and mass transport improve densification and reduce residual porosity.
Improved densification reduces pathways through which a liquid plating bath can infiltrate the ceramic.
Reduced plating-bath infiltration mitigates hole development and component failure during service.
Si-doped ZrB2 sintered near 2000 °C will have similar or enhanced mechanical integrity relative to conventional ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C.
Si-doped ZrB2 will develop significantly fewer porosity-related defects during liquid plating exposure than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 typically has higher porosity than the proposed Si-doped material.
Conventionally prepared ZrB2 is prone to hole formation during long-term exposure to a liquid plating bath.
The proposed preparation window is a sintering cycle peaking near 2000 °C.
The relevant service boundary is prolonged exposure to a controlled liquid plating bath.
Silicon may cause unanticipated phase formation or interfacial reactions that affect performance.
Density and porosity can be compared using Archimedes' method and microscopic imaging.
Mechanical integrity can be assessed using flexural strength and hardness measurements.
Phase constitution and grain-boundary structure can be assessed by XRD and microscopy.

The hypothesis is falsified if Si-doped samples show neither a statistically significant reduction in porosity or hole size and number nor at least comparable mechanical and long-duration bath integrity.
